description:
The Khatwari Darbar is among the most celebrated of the historic Sikh and Nanakpanthi shrines of Shikarpur, the north-Sindh town once known as the "Paris of Sindh" for the wealth of its merchant houses. It is traditionally held to have been founded by Bhai Gurdas Singh — also remembered by the name Kanhiya Lal — a disciple of Guru Gobind Singh who, after the Guru's death in 1708, is said to have travelled to Sindh and preached the Sikh teaching at Shikarpur. He is remembered as delivering his sermons seated upon a *khat* (a rope cot), from which the darbar took its name, "Khatwari". The building most likely dates to the second quarter of the eighteenth century and is one of the finest structures in the town: a two-storey *haveli*-style darbar noted for its fresco paintings and intricate woodwork, decoration rarely matched elsewhere in upper Sindh. Images of the ten Sikh Gurus adorn its walls, and three doorways open onto the main hall, where the *Guru Granth Sahib* is installed. The darbar belongs to the shared Nanakpanthi and *Udasi* devotional world of Sindh, in which Sindhi Hindus and Sikhs venerated the Gurus together. There are in fact three Khatwari Darbars in Shikarpur — the principal one, or Khatwari Dharamshala, in Thekrati Bazar — and the tradition of Bhai Gurdas is also remembered at Shahdadkot and at Gandava in Jhal Magsi.

Local tradition, as recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, adds a specific origin story: Guru Gobind Singh is said to have found Bhai Gurdas serving water to wounded Muslim and Sikh soldiers alike, and instructed him to carry the teaching to Shikarpur. The darbar's hall houses, alongside the *Guru Granth Sahib*, an image of Sri Chand — Guru Nanak's eldest son — and the *Jyot*, or sacred light, of Jhulelal, binding the shrine into Sindh's wider devotional world. The building was originally five storeys and is now reduced to two; its two entrances carry marble images of Durga and of Ganpati flanked by his two wives, and its central door bears ten carved panels of Sikh Gurus and saints, including Baba Sewa Das and Baba Kashi Das. By 2018 its mural paintings were reported in advanced decay and its ornate wooden doors sold off to dealers, and the darbar's once-extensive precinct has shrunk to a few buildings, with its former Vidyalaya now rebuilt as a charity hospital; a branch was also established in Mumbai after Partition. The darbar's continued existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib were independently confirmed in 2013, when it was named among Sindh shrines hit by a wave of reported desecrations.

## Bibliography

- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," *Youlin Magazine*, 6 June 2024.
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Gurus in Shikarpur," *The Friday Times*, 12 January 2018.
- Staff Reporter, "Desecration of Guru Granth Sahib across Sindh cities slammed," *Dawn*, 28 August 2013.
qa_note: The addition above draws on two articles by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro (The Friday Times, 2018; Youlin Magazine, 2024) and an independent 2013 Dawn report confirming the darbar's existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib. Several points remain unresolved across the sources: Kalhoro's own two articles spell the founder's original name differently ("Kanhiya Lal" in 2024 vs "Kanya Lal" in 2018); the 2024 article records an alternative tradition that Bhai Gurdas first preached at Gandava in Balochistan, not Shikarpur; and a Wikipedia passage (not independently verified) describes the darbar as dedicated to Bhai Kanhaiya, the Sewapanthi founder, whose water-carrier story is similar to but distinct from the one told here of Bhai Gurdas — the relationship between the two figures could not be resolved in this research pass. The detailed architectural and biographical material rests substantially on Kalhoro's own scholarship; only the darbar's bare existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib have independent corroboration.
